newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury's international clout is growing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury's international clout is growing.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

Treasury official David Lipton was at the home of a Mexican millionaire discussing that country's future when he received an urgent phone call from the State Department's Richard Holbrooke in Dayton, Ohio.

Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic was threatening to sabotage the Yugoslav peace talks if Serbia did not get relief from Western economic sanctions and Holbrooke asked Lipton to come to Dayton to contain the damage.

Thrust in the unusual role of foreign diplomat, the Treasury official succeeded in winning Milosevic's trust -- the Serbian leader wound up calling Lipton a fellow banker -- and helped bring the Nov. 1995 talks to a successful end.

As President Clinton prepares to meet this week with his fellow leaders of the industrial world, Lipton and other Treasury officials are playing increasingly important roles in areas once reserved for the State Department and the Pentagon.

In early April, Robert Rubin became the first U.S. Treasury Secretary to visit Vietnam, where he signed a debt deal but also reviewed the status of Americans still missing in action in the war with Hanoi that ended 22 years ago.

Later that same month, Rubin's deputy, Lawrence Summers, went before the U.S. Chamber of Commerce to tout the economic benefits of the enlargement of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization military alliance.

Administration officials and private analysts ascribe the Treasury's growing influence in the international arena to a variety of factors. Some may be temporary, such as the State Department's preoccupation with the Middle East in Clinton's first term. Others though seem more long-lasting.
"Many of the key security challenges of the post Cold War era are economic and financial," Deputy Treasury Secretary Summers told Reuters in an interview.

That is true in countries as seemingly diverse as Haiti and Russia, both of which are struggling to build democratic societies and stabilize their economies and where the Treasury Department has played a key role in fashioning U.S. policy.

"When tax collections are a crucial element of dialogue between the United States and Russia because of the consequences of hyper-inflation in Russia or a failure to pay money due to the military, it is inevitable Treasury will be drawn in," Summers said.
Administration officials said that President Clinton's determination to elevate the role of economics in the foreign policy arena has also played to Treasury's advantage.

So too has Treasury's role as U.S. representative at the the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. As Washington has cut back on bilateral foreign aid, the IMF and World Bank have become more important as financiers of developing countries and the nations of the former Communist bloc.

The Treasury's growing clout has led to some grumbling at other government departments that have seen their influence wane. Summers was described by one administration official as "no shrinking violet", although he seems a much smoother operator than when Clinton first took office in 1993.

Treasury officials deny they are out to run roughshod over other government agencies and instead paint a picture of an administration where departments are less concerned with protecting turf than in working together to solve problems.

Administration officials said Treasury has benefited from weaknesses at other government agencies. The State Department under former Secretary Warren Christopher concentrated on the Middle East and gave short shrift to international economics.

After a strong start under the late Ron Brown, the Commerce Department has been preoccupied with fighting off Congressional efforts first to dismantle it and then to implicate it in campaign financing scandals.

And the National Economic Council at the White House -- which coordinates administration economic policy -- has arguably never been as powerful since the influential Rubin left it for Treasury 2-1/2 years ago.
"Treasury is spreading its wings in a vacuum," was how one administration official put it.
Economic analyst Stefan-Gotz Richter, head of Transatlantic Futures, described Treasury's growing influence as "the ultimate power grab" but welcomed it nonetheless.
In the post Cold War era where U.S. involvement overseas has to be justified on economic, rather than military grounds, Treasury is best placed to make the case, he said.
"That is why on most U.S. hot spots -- Mexico, Russia and even Vietnam -- the Treasury's role before and behind the scenes just keeps on rising," Richter said.
